Canada's Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Tax Incentive Program is the single largest federal source of support for industrial research and experimental development in the country. According to CRA statistics reported by Canadian tax practitioners, the agency allowed $4.6 billion in Investment Tax Credits (ITCs) across 23,677 processed claims in the 2025–2026 fiscal year, and official CRA program updates confirm that small businesses accounted for 65% of all SR&ED claims submitted during that period. Between December 2024 and November 2026, the federal SR&ED landscape and provincial R&D regimes underwent their most consequential statutory restructuring in over a decade. At the federal level, Bill C-15 (Budget 2025 Implementation Act, No. 1, S.C. 2026, c. 3), which received Royal Assent on March 26, 2026, enacted sweeping enhancements effective retroactively to taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024. These enacted reforms doubled the annual expenditure limit for the enhanced 35% refundable ITC from $3 million to $6 million (raising the maximum annual federal cash refund on current expenditures from $1,050,000 to $2,100,000), expanded the prior-year taxable capital phase-out thresholds from $10 million–$50 million to $15 million–$75 million, introduced an elective three-year average gross revenue phase-out mechanism, extended the enhanced 35% refundable ITC to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs), and restored SR&ED eligibility for capital expenditures, Shared-Use Equipment (SUE), and equipment lease costs incurred after December 15, 2024. Concurrently, the CRA launched an optional Pre-Claim Approval regime on April 1, 2026, while Québec abolished seven legacy R&D tax credits for taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025, consolidating its provincial support into the new 20%–30% refundable Tax Credit for R&D, Innovation and Pre-Commercialization (CRIC).
1. Executive Summary and Audit of 2024–2026 Legislative Reforms

A rigorous audit of circulating R&D tax literature in Canada reveals frequent reliance on superseded statutory parameters—most notably outdated references to the pre-2013 65% Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) rate, the pre-December 16, 2024 $3 million expenditure limit, the post-2013 capital expenditure prohibition, and abolished Québec salary and university tax credits. Furthermore, early technical summaries published between late 2024 and mid-2025 frequently cite an interim $4.5 million expenditure limit proposed in the 2024 Fall Economic Statement and reflected in the August 2025 Department of Finance draft legislative proposals. That interim figure was subsequently superseded when Federal Budget 2025 and the December 2025 Notice of Ways and Means Motion increased the statutory expenditure limit to $6 million prior to final enactment in Bill C-15 on March 26, 2026.

body.text: In addition to the enacted Bill C-15 provisions, Federal Budget 2026 introduced a major policy expansion proposing to extend SR&ED eligibility to commercialization expenses—specifically expenditures associated with bringing a new product or process to market, including obtaining mandatory regulatory approvals or certifications and securing and maintaining intellectual property (IP) protection. This Budget 2026 measure is projected in Chapter 1 of the federal budget plan to deliver $930 million in fiscal support over five years ($235 million ongoing) and applies to expenditures incurred in taxation years beginning on or after Budget Day 2026, with sector-specific administrative guidance forthcoming from the CRA.
2. Statutory and Legislative Architecture of the Federal SR&ED Program

The Canadian SR&ED tax incentive regime operates through a dual-benefit statutory mechanism embedded within the federal Income Tax Act (R.S.C., 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.)) and Part XXIX of the Income Tax Regulations (C.R.C., c. 945). First, taxpayers carrying on a business in Canada may pool and deduct allowable current and capital SR&ED expenditures against business income in the current taxation year or carry those unused deductions forward indefinitely under section 37 of the Act. Second, taxpayers may earn an Investment Tax Credit (ITC) on their "qualified expenditures" under section 127 and section 127.1 of the Act, which reduces Part I federal income tax otherwise payable, generates a direct cash refund, or both.
2.1 Subsection 248(1): Statutory Definitions

The foundational legal definitions governing SR&ED eligibility and expenditure limits are codified in subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act. Under subsection 248(1), "scientific research and experimental development" means a systematic investigation or search that is carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis and that falls into one of three core categories: (a) basic research, namely, work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge without a specific practical application in view; (b) applied research, namely, work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge with a specific practical application in view; or (c) experimental development, namely, work undertaken for the purpose of achieving technological advancement for the purpose of creating new, or improving existing, materials, devices, products or processes, including incremental improvements thereto. Paragraph (d) of the definition includes support work with respect to engineering, design, operations research, mathematical analysis, computer programming, data collection, testing, or psychological research, where the work is commensurate with the needs, and directly in support, of work described in paragraph (a), (b), or (c) that is undertaken in Canada. Paragraphs (e) through (k) enumerate seven specific categories of excluded commercial, social science, resource extraction, and routine activities.

Subsection 248(1) also defines the key payroll and entity concepts that govern SR&ED expenditure calculations. The term "salary or wages" (except in sections 5 and 63 and the definition of "death benefit") means the income of a taxpayer from an office or employment as computed under subdivision a of Division B of Part I of the Act, and includes all fees received for services not rendered in the course of the taxpayer's business, vacation pay, statutory holiday pay, sick leave pay, bonuses, commissions, and taxable benefits under section 6, but excludes superannuation or pension benefits or retiring allowances. A "specified employee" of a person is defined in subsection 248(1) as an employee who is a specified shareholder of the person—meaning a taxpayer who owns, directly or indirectly, at any time in the year, not less than 10% of the issued shares of any class of the capital stock of the corporation or of any corporation related to the corporation—or who does not deal at arm's length with the employer. Finally, a "specified member" of a partnership is defined in subsection 248(1) as any member who is a limited partner (within the meaning of subsection 96(2.4)) at any time during the partnership's fiscal period, or any member (other than a limited partner) who, while a partner, was not regularly, continuously, and substantially during the partnership's fiscal period actively engaged in the activities of the partnership's business (except for the financing of the partnership) or carrying on a business similar to that of the partnership. Under the partnership rules in subsections 96(1) and 127(8), specified members are strictly barred from claiming partnership SR&ED ITCs.
2.2 Section 37: The Pool of Deductible SR&ED Expenditures

Subsection 37(1) creates a running cumulative account—the Pool of Deductible SR&ED Expenditures—for any taxpayer carrying on a business in Canada in a taxation year. Unlike ordinary business expenses deducted annually under section 9, allowable SR&ED expenditures added to the subsection 37(1) pool may be deducted in full, in part, or retained in the pool and carried forward indefinitely to reduce income from the business in any future taxation year.
Additions to the Subsection 37(1) Pool

The pool is increased by the aggregate of the statutory additions set out in paragraphs 37(1)(a) through 37(1)(c.3). Paragraph 37(1)(a) adds expenditures of a current nature made in the year or a preceding taxation year across five specific subparagraphs: subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i) covers current expenditures on SR&ED carried on in Canada, directly undertaken by the taxpayer, and related to a business of the taxpayer; subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i.01) covers current expenditures on SR&ED carried on in Canada directly undertaken on behalf of the taxpayer (contract SR&ED expenditures) and related to a business of the taxpayer; subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i.1) covers third-party payments to a corporation resident in Canada ("Type A Entity") to be used for SR&ED carried on in Canada related to a business of the taxpayer, provided the taxpayer is entitled to exploit the results; subparagraph 37(1)(a)(ii) covers third-party payments to approved entities where the taxpayer is entitled to exploit the results of SR&ED related to its business—namely, Clause (A) an approved association that undertakes SR&ED ("Type B Entity"), Clause (B) an approved university, college, research institute, or other similar institution ("Type C Entity"), Clause (C) a non-profit SR&ED corporation resident in Canada and exempt from tax under paragraph 149(1)(j) ("Type D Entity"), or Clause (E) an approved organization (granting council) that makes payments to an association, institution, or corporation described in Clauses (A) to (C) ("Type E Entity"), while Clause (D) was repealed in 1996 (S.C. 1996, c. 21, s. 9(4)); and subparagraph 37(1)(a)(iii) covers corporate payments to a corporation resident in Canada exempt from tax under paragraph 149(1)(j) ("Type F Entity") for basic or applied research carried on in Canada that has the potential for technological application in other businesses unrelated to the taxpayer's business, where the primary purpose of the payment is to enable the taxpayer to use the results in conjunction with other SR&ED undertaken directly by or on behalf of the taxpayer.

Enacted by Bill C-15 (S.C. 2026, c. 3) to reverse the post-2013 repeal, paragraph 37(1)(b) adds expenditures of a capital nature made in the year or a preceding taxation year on SR&ED carried on in Canada, directly undertaken by or on behalf of the taxpayer and related to the taxpayer's business, for property acquired after December 15, 2024 that would otherwise be depreciable property of the taxpayer (excluding land, a leasehold interest in land, a building, or a leasehold interest in a building, unless it is a prescribed special-purpose building under Regulation 2903). Under subsection 37(1.2), a capital expenditure under paragraph 37(1)(b) is deemed not to have been made until the property becomes "available for use" by the taxpayer. Under subsection 37(6), any amount claimed under subsection 37(1) in respect of paragraph 37(1)(b) capital expenditures is deemed to be an amount allowed to the taxpayer in respect of the property under Capital Cost Allowance (CCA) regulations (paragraph 20(1)(a)) as a separate prescribed class. Finally, the pool is increased by paragraph 37(1)(c) for repayments of government or non-government assistance that previously reduced the pool under paragraph 37(1)(d); paragraph 37(1)(c.1) for all amounts included in computing the taxpayer's income for a preceding taxation year under paragraph 12(1)(v) (which brings a negative year-end pool balance into taxable income, resetting the opening pool balance to nil for the following year); and paragraphs 37(1)(c.2) and 37(1)(c.3) for amounts added to tax payable in a preceding taxation year under the ITC recapture rules of subsections 127(27), 127(29), or 127(34) (para 37(1)(c.2)), or excess partnership recapture amounts under subsection 127(30) for any preceding fiscal period (para 37(1)(c.3)).
Subtractions from the Subsection 37(1) Pool

The subsection 37(1) pool is reduced by the aggregate of the statutory deductions in paragraphs 37(1)(d) through 37(1)(h). Paragraph 37(1)(d) deducts all amounts of government assistance or non-government assistance (as defined in subsection 127(9)) in respect of an expenditure described in paragraph 37(1)(a) or 37(1)(b) that, at the taxpayer's filing-due date for the year, the taxpayer has received, is entitled to receive, or can reasonably be expected to receive. Paragraph 37(1)(d.1) deducts all provincial super-allowance benefit amounts for the year or a preceding taxation year. Paragraph 37(1)(e) deducts all federal SR&ED ITC amounts deducted under subsection 127(5) (including refundable ITCs deemed deducted under subsection 127(5)) in computing tax payable for a preceding taxation year, to the extent the ITC can reasonably be considered attributable to a Prescribed Proxy Amount, a current expenditure, or a capital expenditure claimed in the pool. If the paragraph 37(1)(e) reduction drives the pool balance negative at year-end, the negative balance must be included in business income for that year under paragraph 12(1)(v) (and paragraph 12(1)(t) to the extent not already applied to reduce the pool or Undepreciated Capital Cost). Paragraphs 37(1)(f) and 37(1)(f.1) deduct amounts previously deducted under subsection 37(1) in preceding taxation years (para 37(1)(f)) and amounts deducted in respect of insolvency under section 61.3 for preceding years (para 37(1)(f.1)), while paragraph 37(1)(g) deducts twice the amount claimed under subparagraph 194(2)(a)(ii) for preceding years. Finally, if a corporation undergoes a "loss restriction event" (an acquisition of control) or a trust gains a new majority-interest beneficiary, paragraph 37(1)(h) and subsection 37(6.1) reduce the unrestricted pool to nil and stream pre-acquisition SR&ED pool balances so they may only be deducted in a subsequent year if the specific business to which the SR&ED expenditures related continues to be carried on for profit or with a reasonable expectation of profit, and only up to the income generated from that same or a similar business.
Specialized Jurisdictional, Corporate, and Administrative Provisions in Section 37

Section 37 contains several targeted provisions governing corporate groups, geographic boundaries, and intellectual property acquisitions. Under subsection 37(1.1), where a corporate taxpayer performs SR&ED related to a business actively carried on by another corporation to which the taxpayer is related (determined without reference to paragraph 251(5)(b) rights), the SR&ED is deemed to relate to a business of the taxpayer. Under subsection 37(1.3), an expenditure made in the course of carrying on a business in Canada for SR&ED conducted in the Exclusive Economic Zone of Canada (as defined in the Oceans Act), or in the airspace above or seabed/subsoil below that zone, is deemed to have been made in Canada. Under subsections 37(1.4) and 37(1.5), salary or wages paid to an employee who was resident in Canada at the time the expense was incurred for SR&ED carried on outside Canada directly undertaken by the taxpayer, related to a business of the taxpayer, and solely in support of SR&ED carried on by the taxpayer in Canada are deemed to be made in Canada up to the lesser of the actual foreign SR&ED wages and 10% of the taxpayer's total Canadian SR&ED salary and wage expenditures directly undertaken in that taxation year, provided the foreign remuneration is not subject to an income or profits tax imposed by another country (subsection 37(9)). Any other current expenditures on SR&ED carried on outside Canada directly undertaken by or on behalf of the taxpayer (beyond the 10% deemed-Canadian wage cap in s. 37(1.4)), or payments to approved foreign universities or research associations, are deductible in computing current-year business income under subsection 37(2), but cannot enter the subsection 37(1) carryforward pool and cannot earn SR&ED ITCs.

Furthermore, subsection 37(3) authorizes the Minister of National Revenue to obtain technical advice from the Department of Industry, the National Research Council of Canada, the Defence Research Board, or any other federal department or agency regarding whether an activity constitutes SR&ED. Subsection 37(4) (together with Regulation 2902(c)) prohibits any deduction under section 37 or any ITC in respect of an expenditure made to acquire rights in, or arising out of, SR&ED, preventing duplication of tax incentives between the original SR&ED performer and a subsequent purchaser of intellectual property. Subsection 37(5) prevents double-deduction under the charitable gift provisions of sections 110.1 or 118.1 for any amount deducted under section 37. Finally, during the 2014–2024 period when capital expenditures were ineligible, former subsection 37(14) (the capital look-through rule) required a payer's SR&ED contract or third-party payment to be reduced by any related non-current (capital or lease) expenditure of the performer, and former subsection 37(15) required the performer to notify the payer in writing within 90 days after calendar year-end. Consequential on the restoration of paragraph 37(1)(b) capital expenditures for property acquired after December 15, 2024, Bill C-15 (S.C. 2026, c. 3, s. 5) repealed subsections 37(14) and 37(15).
2.3 Part XXIX of the Income Tax Regulations (Sections 2900 to 2903)

Part XXIX of the Income Tax Regulations prescribes the detailed rules for computing SR&ED overhead, the Prescribed Proxy Amount, Shared-Use Equipment exclusions, and non-qualifying prescribed expenditures. Under subsection 2900(2) (applicable to the Traditional Method under clause 37(8)(a)(i)(B) and subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(II) of the Act), three categories of expenditures are prescribed as directly attributable to the prosecution of SR&ED: (a) the cost of materials consumed or transformed in such prosecution; (b) where an employee directly undertakes, supervises, or supports such prosecution, the portion of salary or wages that can reasonably be considered to be in respect of such prosecution; and (c) other expenditures (or portions thereof) that are directly related to such prosecution and that would not have been incurred if such prosecution had not occurred (the incremental test). Subsection 2900(3) prescribes expenditures directly attributable to the provision of premises, facilities, or equipment for the prosecution of SR&ED under the Traditional Method: (a) the cost of maintenance and upkeep of such premises, facilities, or equipment; and (b) other expenditures (or portions thereof) directly related to that provision that would not have been incurred if those premises, facilities, or equipment had not existed.

For taxpayers electing the Proxy Method under clause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B) of the Act, subsection 2900(4) establishes that the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) for the purposes of the "qualified expenditure" definition in subsection 127(9) is 55% of the total of all eligible portions of salaries and wages of employees directly engaged in SR&ED in Canada. Under subsection 2900(5), where the portion of an employee's directly engaged SR&ED salary or wages under subsection 2900(4) is "all or substantially all" (90% or more) of their total salary or wages, that portion is replaced by 100% of the expenditure, subject to subsections 2900(6) to (8). Subsection 2900(6) imposes the Overall Cap on the PPA so that it cannot exceed total business operating deductions minus specified statutory deductions (sections 20, 24, 26, 30, 32, 37, 66–66.8, and 104) and non-special-purpose building outlays. Subsections 2900(7) to 2900(10) restrict the salary base of a specified employee to the lesser of 75% of total salary/wages and 2.5 × YMPE × (days ÷ 365) (s. 2900(7)), mandate sharing of the 2.5 × YMPE limit across associated corporations (s. 2900(8) and 2900(10)), and exclude taxable benefits (sections 6 and 7), bonuses, remuneration based on profits, and subsection 78(4) prior-year unpaid wages from the salary base of all employees (s. 2900(9)).

With respect to capital property, subsection 2900(11) defines Prescribed Depreciable Property (PDP), excluding property from qualifying as Shared-Use Equipment (SUE) if, at the time of acquisition, the claimant intended to use it for SR&ED during the assembly, construction, or commissioning of a commercial manufacturing, processing, or other commercial facility, plant, or line (para 2900(11)(c)) and intended to use it during its operating time in its expected useful life primarily for purposes other than SR&ED (subpara 2900(11)(c)(i)). Section 2902 enumerates prescribed expenditures that are excluded from "qualified expenditures" and cannot earn ITCs, including general administrative or management salaries and benefits (unless ASA or directly attributable), legal or accounting fees, interest and financing costs under paragraphs 20(1)(c) to (g), entertainment expenses, advertising or selling expenses, conference or convention expenses, dues or fees for membership in scientific or technical societies, fines or penalties, fees for preparing SR&ED claims (para 2902(a)), used capital property (para 2902(b)), and acquisition of SR&ED rights (para 2902(c)). Finally, section 2903 (amended consequential to Bill C-15) defines what constitutes a "prescribed special-purpose building" eligible for SR&ED capital and lease deductions under paragraphs 37(1)(b) and 37(8)(e).
3. Technical Eligibility Criteria and CRA Administrative Guidelines ("Why" and "How")

For an expenditure to qualify for federal SR&ED tax incentives, the underlying technical work must satisfy the definition of "scientific research and experimental development" in subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act. What is generally understood in commercial industry to be "research and development" (R&D) or engineering product development is not necessarily "SR&ED" within the meaning of the Act.
3.1 Evolution from the "Five Questions" to the "Why and How" Framework

For nearly two decades following the landmark 1998 Tax Court of Canada decision in Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Limited v. The Queen, the CRA evaluated technical eligibility using Five Questions codified in the Eligibility of Work for SR&ED Investment Tax Credits Policy (first published in 2012, revised in April 2015, and archived in August 2021). On August 13, 2021, following a 2020 modernization initiative, the CRA replaced the 2015 policy with the Guidelines on the Eligibility of Work for SR&ED Tax Incentives, which consolidated the five questions into Two Requirements: the "Why" Requirement and the "How" Requirement.

Both the CRA and the Federal Court of Appeal (in National R&D Inc. v. Canada, 2022 FCA 72) have confirmed that the 2021 "Why and How" Guidelines did not alter the substantive legal test for SR&ED; rather, both frameworks derive directly from the unchanged text of subsection 248(1) and the binding judicial criteria of Northwest Hydraulic.

body.text: 3.2 Deep Dive into the "Why" Requirement: Uncertainty and Advancement

To satisfy the "Why" Requirement, the claimant must demonstrate that the impetus for the work was a scientific or technological uncertainty and that the targeted outcome was a scientific or technological advancement. The CRA Guidelines emphasize that SR&ED seeks to generate or discover conceptual knowledge—such as explanatory theories, principles, or prediction models that explain why a material, device, or system behaves in a particular manner—rather than purely factual knowledge such as routine physical measurements or raw data observations.

A scientific or technological uncertainty arises when it is unknown or uncertain whether a given result or objective can be achieved, or how to achieve it, because the available scientific or technological knowledge base (comprising both internal resources within the business and knowledge publicly or reasonably available in the field) is insufficient. Common characteristics indicating an insufficiency in technological knowledge include situations where existing design methods are inapplicable, specifications or requirements do not conform to existing engineering standards, there are too many interacting variables or unknowns (systemic uncertainty), or operating parameters fall outside normal ranges. Conversely, if a technical problem is circumvented using an existing workaround, or resolved by acquiring available knowledge through training, on-the-job learning, hiring expert employees or consultants, or purchasing proprietary know-how, the work does not meet the requirement of attempting to achieve a technological advancement. Crucially, whether a project succeeds or fails in achieving its commercial or technical objective is irrelevant to SR&ED eligibility; an abandoned or failed experiment fully qualifies if the purpose of the work was to achieve a scientific or technological advancement by resolving a genuine uncertainty.
3.3 Deep Dive into the "How" Requirement: Systematic Investigation and Contemporaneous Evidence

To satisfy the "How" Requirement, the work must be conducted by qualified individuals through a systematic investigation or search in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis. Under the CRA Guidelines, a systematic investigation requires four sequential methodological elements:

items: Formulating an Initial Idea or Hypothesis: Generating an idea consistent with known scientific or technological facts that serves as a starting point for further investigation toward achieving the objective or resolving the problem, expressed as a proposed method, approach, or causal hypothesis.

Testing by Experiment or Analysis: Testing the idea or hypothesis systematically by means of controlled experiment or analysis, allowing the hypothesis to evolve and change iteratively as empirical results are obtained.
Developing Logical Conclusions: Formulating reasoned, logical conclusions based on the empirical results or analytical findings of the experiments.

Keeping Contemporaneous Evidence: Retaining evidence generated continuously as the work progresses—such as dated engineering or laboratory notebooks, Git version-control commit logs referencing specific SR&ED projects, Jira/Asana/Notion project tickets, test bench data, photographs or videos of prototype iterations, and physical scrap.

body.text: 3.4 Categories of Eligible Work, the Eight Support Work Categories, and Statutory Exclusions

Under subsection 248(1), once a valid SR&ED project is established around a core of Basic Research (para 248(1)(a)), Applied Research (para 248(1)(b)), or Experimental Development (para 248(1)(c)—the most common category claimed by Canadian businesses), the boundary of the eligible project extends to include Support Work (para 248(1)(d)). Support work is not SR&ED standing on its own; it derives its eligibility strictly from supporting an underlying basic research, applied research, or experimental development project. To qualify under paragraph 248(1)(d), support work must be commensurate with the needs and directly in support of core SR&ED undertaken in Canada, and must fall within one of eight exhaustive statutory categories: (1) engineering, (2) design, (3) operations research, (4) mathematical analysis, (5) computer programming, (6) data collection, (7) testing, or (8) psychological research.

Conversely, paragraphs 248(1)(e) through (k) explicitly exclude seven categories of work from the definition of SR&ED, which must be segregated and removed from any claim: (e) market research or sales promotion; (f) quality control or routine testing of materials, devices, products, or processes; (g) research in the social sciences or the humanities; (h) prospecting, exploring, or drilling for, or producing, minerals, petroleum, or natural gas; (i) the commercial production of a new or improved material, device, or product, or the commercial use of a new or improved process; (j) style changes; and (k) routine data collection.

As the CRA Guidelines highlight, activities such as "data collection" and "testing" appear in both paragraph (d) (eligible support work) and paragraphs (f) and (k) (excluded work). The decisive legal distinction is purpose: if data collection or testing is carried out specifically and directly to test a hypothesis and resolve an SR&ED uncertainty, it qualifies as eligible support work under paragraph (d); if it is performed for routine commercial quality control or standard business operations, it is excluded under paragraphs (f) or (k). Similarly, under the CRA's SR&ED During Production Runs Policy, when experimental development takes place in a commercial manufacturing facility, the CRA distinguishes between Experimental Development with Experimental Production (ED+EP)—where a trial production run is required for SR&ED and direct labour and materials consumed are allowable (excluding any excess production)—and Experimental Development Simultaneous with Commercial Production (ED+CP), where all normal commercial production costs must be excluded and only the incremental excess costs attributable to the experimental development work are allowable.
4. Federal Investment Tax Credit (ITC) Rates, Expenditure Limits, Refundability, and Carryovers
4.1 Basic (15%) and Enhanced (35%) Federal ITC Rates

The federal SR&ED Program provides two tiers of Investment Tax Credit rates under section 127 of the Income Tax Act. First, the basic ITC rate of 15% under subsection 127(9) is available to all taxable Canadian claimants—including non-qualifying corporations, foreign-controlled subsidiaries, large corporations exceeding their expenditure limit phase-out, sole proprietors (individuals), partners of partnerships, and beneficiaries of trusts—on qualified SR&ED expenditures that do not qualify for the enhanced rate. Second, under subsection 127(10.1), qualifying Canadian-Controlled Private Corporations (CCPCs) and, for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) earn an additional 20% ITC on top of the 15% basic rate, producing a combined 35% enhanced ITC rate on qualified SR&ED expenditures up to their annual Expenditure Limit.
4.2 The $6 Million Expenditure Limit and Phase-Out Mechanics (CCPCs and ECPCs)

For taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, Bill C-15 doubled the maximum annual Expenditure Limit from $3,000,000 to $6,000,000. Because eligibility follows the start date of the taxation year rather than the year-end, a calendar-year corporation whose taxation year began on January 1, 2025, or January 1, 2026, qualifies for the $6,000,000 limit, whereas a corporation with a fiscal year running from December 1, 2024 to November 30, 2025 remained subject to the $3,000,000 limit for that entire fiscal period. Tax years shorter than 51 weeks receive a prorated expenditure limit based on the number of days in the short taxation year divided by 365 (for example, a 273-day short taxation year receives an expenditure limit of $4,487,671 instead of $6,000,000).
A. CCPC Taxable Capital Phase-Out Formula (Subsection 127(10.2))

By default, a CCPC's $6,000,000 expenditure limit phases out linearly when the taxable capital employed in Canada (within the meaning of former Part I.3 of the Act) of the corporation—and all CCPCs in its associated group under section 256—for the immediately preceding taxation year exceeds $15,000,000, reaching nil at $75,000,000. The statutory formula under subsection 127(10.2) is:
Expenditure Limit = Base Limit × (Phase-Out Range − A) / (Phase-Out Range)
Expenditure Limit = Base Limit × (Phase-Out Range − A) ÷ Phase-Out Range

Under the enacted post-December 15, 2024 parameters, the Base Limit is $6,000,000, the Phase-Out Range is $60,000,000, and variable A is the prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada in excess of $15,000,000 (capped at a maximum excess of $60,000,000, and equal to $0 if prior-year taxable capital is $15,000,000 or less), so that Expenditure Limit = $6,000,000 × ($60,000,000 − A) ÷ $60,000,000. Under this formula, every $1,000,000 of prior-year taxable capital above $15,000,000 reduces the $6,000,000 expenditure limit by $100,000 (and reduces the maximum $2,100,000 enhanced credit by $35,000). Following Bill C-15, the SR&ED taxable capital phase-out ($15M to $75M) is now decoupled from the federal Small Business Deduction (SBD) taxable capital phase-out ($10M to $50M). Associated CCPCs must share a single $6,000,000 expenditure limit (s. 127(10.21) and s. 127(10.3)) and allocate it using Schedule T2SCH49 (Agreement Among Associated Corporations to Allocate the Expenditure Limit). Under subsection 127(10.5) (formerly numbered 127(10.6)), specific proration rules apply when a CCPC has more than one taxation year ending in the same calendar year and is associated with another CCPC in two or more of those years.
B. Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) and CCPC Revenue Election (Subsections 127(10.6), 127(10.31), and 127(10.32))

Bill C-15 amended subsection 127(9) and added subsections 127(10.6) to 127(10.64) to extend the enhanced 35% ITC up to the $6,000,000 expenditure limit to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs)—broadly defined as corporations resident in Canada whose shares are listed on a designated stock exchange in Canada (or eligible subsidiaries thereof) and that are not controlled by non-residents.

Because public corporations frequently carry higher balance-sheet equity that would distort a taxable capital test, subsection 127(10.6) calculates an ECPC's expenditure limit using the same $6,000,000 × ($60,000,000 − A) ÷ $60,000,000 formula structure, except variable A is based on the corporation's average annual gross revenue reflected in its financial statements over the three preceding fiscal years in excess of $15,000,000, phasing out completely at $75,000,000 (a $60,000,000 phase-out range). If the ECPC is a member of a "consolidated group" (defined in subsection 127(9) and cross-referencing subsection 233.8(1) as a group in respect of which an ultimate parent entity prepares, or would be required on a public securities exchange to prepare, consolidated financial statements presenting assets, liabilities, income, expenses, and cash flows as a single economic entity), the $6,000,000 expenditure limit is calculated using the consolidated group's three-year average annual revenue (s. 127(10.61)) and must be shared across all consolidated ECPC members (s. 127(10.62)) via new Schedule T2SCH52 (Agreement Among Consolidated Eligible Canadian Public Corporations or Electing Associated Canadian-Controlled Private Corporations to Allocate the Expenditure Limit). If a consolidated ECPC group (or associated CCPC group) fails to file an allocation agreement within 30 days after a ministerial request, the Minister of National Revenue allocates the expenditure limit among the group under subsection 127(10.63) (or subsection 127(10.4) for CCPCs).

Crucially, for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, a standalone CCPC (under subsection 127(10.31)) or an associated group of CCPCs (under subsection 127(10.32)) may elect to calculate its expenditure limit using the three-year average annual gross revenue method under subsection 127(10.6) instead of the taxable capital method under subsection 127(10.2). This election is made on Schedule T2SCH31 (Line 383 and Lines 387–389) and, for associated CCPCs, Schedule T2SCH52. This provides major relief to capital-intensive, pre-revenue, or low-revenue Canadian biotech, cleantech, and deep-tech startups that have raised over $15 million in equity or convertible debt financing (which inflates taxable capital) but have under $15 million in three-year average revenue.

body.text: Whether a CCPC earns a 40% cash refund on the 15% basic ITC for expenditures above its Expenditure Limit depends on whether it is a "qualifying corporation" (other than an "excluded corporation") as defined in subsection 127.1(2). A CCPC is a qualifying corporation if its taxable income for the immediately preceding taxation year (combined with the taxable incomes of all associated corporations for their preceding taxation years) does not exceed its Qualifying Income Limit (QIL). For taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, Bill C-15 updated the QIL phase-out denominator from $40,000,000 to $60,000,000, so that Qualifying Income Limit = $500,000 × ($60,000,000 − A) ÷ $60,000,000, where A is the prior-year taxable capital in excess of $15,000,000 (up to $60,000,000). Note that under subsection 127.1(2.01), even if a CCPC's prior-year taxable income exceeds its Qualifying Income Limit (meaning it is not a "qualifying corporation"), it still receives the 100% refund on current expenditures and 40% refund on capital expenditures for the 35% enhanced ITC earned within its $6,000,000 Expenditure Limit; the Qualifying Income Limit only restricts the 40% refundability of the 15% basic ITC earned above the expenditure limit.

body.text: 4.5 Carryover Periods and Taxability of Federal ITCs

Under subsections 127(5) and 127(9), any non-refundable SR&ED ITC (or any refundable ITC that the claimant elects not to have refunded) that is not deducted against current-year Part I tax may be carried back 3 taxation years or carried forward 20 taxation years to reduce Part I federal tax otherwise payable. Under subsection 127(5), any SR&ED ITC refunded in cash under section 127.1 is deemed to have been deducted against Part I tax otherwise payable in the year and therefore cannot also be carried back or forward.

Furthermore, federal SR&ED ITCs deducted against Part I tax or refunded in cash in a given taxation year (Year 1) reduce the claimant's Pool of Deductible SR&ED Expenditures in the following taxation year (Year 2) under paragraph 37(1)(e) (or reduce the Undepreciated Capital Cost of Shared-Use Equipment in Year 2 under subsection 13(21)). If the paragraph 37(1)(e) reduction causes the subsection 37(1) pool to become negative at the end of Year 2 (or if the claimant has already deducted its entire subsection 37(1) pool in Year 1 and has no Year 2 pool additions), the negative pool balance is included in the claimant's taxable business income in Year 2 under paragraph 12(1)(v) (and paragraph 12(1)(t)). Thus, federal SR&ED ITCs benefit from a one-year deferral before reducing deductible expenses or increasing taxable income, whereas provincial R&D tax credits reduce federal QREs and the subsection 37(1) pool in the current year (Year 1) as government assistance.
5. Qualifying Expenditures (QREs), Calculation Methods, and Specific Cost Rules
5.1 Election Between the Proxy Method and Traditional Method

Under subsection 37(8) of the Income Tax Act and section 2900 of the Income Tax Regulations, a claimant must elect annually on Form T661 Part 3, Section A whether to compute its SR&ED expenditures using the Proxy Method (Line 160, clause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)) or the Traditional Method (Line 162, clause 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)). The choice of method must be made when Form T661 is first filed for the taxation year and is irrevocable for that year; a taxpayer cannot switch methods retroactively on an amended return. If a claimant fails to select a method on Form T661, the CRA automatically processes the claim using the Traditional Method. If the claimant is a partnership, an election to use the Proxy Method is valid only if made by an authorized partner on behalf of all members of the partnership.

body.text: 5.2 Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) Mechanics and Overall Cap

When a claimant elects the Proxy Method, subsection 2900(4) of the Income Tax Regulations sets the Prescribed Proxy Amount at 55% of the claimant's eligible SR&ED Salary Base (reduced from 65% for 2012 and prior years, and 60% for 2013). The Salary Base in Part 5 of Form T661 includes only the portion of salaries and wages of employees directly engaged in SR&ED in Canada (plus permissible foreign wages under s. 37(1.4)), incurred and paid in the tax year or within 180 days of year-end. For all employees (whether specified or non-specified), subsection 2900(9) strictly excludes from the Salary Base: (1) taxable benefits under section 6; (2) stock option benefits under section 7; (3) bonuses; (4) remuneration based on profits; and (5) prior-year unpaid remuneration paid in the current year (Line 310).

To ensure that a single-purpose R&D business with minimal actual overhead does not claim a notional 55% PPA that causes total tax deductions and PPA to exceed its actual total business outlays, subsection 2900(6) imposes an Overall Cap on the PPA expressed as Overall Cap = A − B − C. In this formula, A is the total of all amounts deducted in computing net income from the business for the year (including Cost of Goods Sold); B is the total of all amounts deducted in computing business income under sections 20 (e.g., CCA, interest, bad debts), 24 (ceasing business), 26 (banks), 30 (farming land improvements), 32 (insurance agents/brokers), 37 (SR&ED pool deductions), 66 to 66.8 (resource exploration/development), and 104 (trusts) of the Act; and C is any amount incurred in the year for the use of, or the right to use, a building other than a prescribed special-purpose building. As the CRA's Prescribed Proxy Amount Policy notes, the overall cap generally does not restrict the PPA for diversified businesses or claimants that deduct more than $55 of non-SR&ED operating expenses (excluding sections 20, 37, and building rent) for every $100 of eligible salary in the salary base.
5.3 Salaries, Wages, and Specified Employee Restrictions
A. Directly Engaged vs. Directly Undertaking, Supervising, or Supporting

Under the Proxy Method, only employees directly engaged in SR&ED may be claimed. This encompasses hands-on scientific/technical personnel, non-specialized shop-floor employees whose work is directly in support of and an integral part of experimental development under qualified technical supervision (section 7.1.1 of the SR&ED Salary or Wages Policy), and first-line managers and supervisors strictly for the portion of their time spent directing the technical course of ongoing SR&ED work or providing direct technical input. Time spent on general corporate management, budgeting, human resources, or administrative oversight is excluded. Under the Traditional Method, clerical and administrative salaries (e.g., an HR recruiter dedicated to hiring SR&ED engineers or purchasing clerks ordering experimental materials) may additionally be claimed on Line 360 if directly related and incremental to the SR&ED, though their related benefits, retiring allowances, training, and travel remain ineligible due to their indirect link to the SR&ED work.
B. Three-Tier Statutory Caps on "Specified Employees" (≥10% Shareholders & Non-Arm's Length)

Where an employee is a specified employee (owning ≥10% of the shares of any class of the corporation or a related corporation, or dealing at non-arm's length with the employer), the Income Tax Act and Income Tax Regulations impose three distinct statutory caps:

items: Absolute Prohibition on Bonuses and Profit-Based Remuneration (ITA Subsection 37(9)): Unlike regular arm's-length employees (whose bonuses and profit-based pay are deductible SR&ED wages on Line 300, though excluded from the Part 5 PPA Salary Base), a specified employee's bonuses and remuneration based on profits are completely excluded from allowable SR&ED salaries and wages under both the Proxy and Traditional methods.

Overall Deductible SR&ED Wage Cap (ITA Subsection 37(9.1)): For the purposes of the subsection 37(1) deductible pool and direct wage claims (Line 305), the maximum SR&ED salary or wages claimable for a specified employee cannot exceed 5 × YMPE × (B ÷ 365), where YMPE is the Year's Maximum Pensionable Earnings (as determined under section 18 of the Canada Pension Plan for the calendar year in which the taxation year ends), and B is the number of days in the taxation year that the individual was a specified employee. Associated corporations must share this limit and file Form T1174 (Agreement Between Associated Corporations to Allocate Salary or Wages of Specified Employees for SR&ED) (subsections 37(9.2) and 37(9.3)).

Proxy Salary Base Dual Cap (ITR Subsections 2900(7) and 2900(8)): For calculating the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount in Part 5 of Form T661, the amount of a specified employee's salary or wages included in the Salary Base cannot exceed the lesser of: (a) 75% of the specified employee's total salary or wages incurred in the year (across both SR&ED and non-SR&ED duties, excluding bonuses, profit-based remuneration, taxable benefits, and prior-year unpaid wages); and (b) 2.5 × A × (B ÷ 365), where A is the YMPE for the calendar year in which the tax year ends, and B is the number of days in the tax year that the claimant employed the individual (with no proration for days the employee was not a specified employee), shared across all associated corporations.

body.text: C. Partner Remuneration Exclusion and the 180-Day Unpaid Remuneration Rule

For income tax purposes, a partner (member) of a partnership cannot be an employee of that partnership; any "salary or wages" paid to a partner is treated by the CRA as a distribution of partnership income and cannot be claimed as an SR&ED salary expenditure. Additionally, a partnership cannot carry forward a subsection 37(1) pool balance to future years and must deduct 100% of its available SR&ED pool in computing partnership net income for the current fiscal period.

Under subsection 78(4) of the Income Tax Act, any employee salary or wages incurred in a taxation year that remain unpaid on the day that is 180 days after the end of the taxation year are deemed not to have been incurred in that year, and are instead deemed to be an expenditure incurred in the subsequent taxation year in which they are actually paid (reported on Line 315 when unpaid and Line 310 when subsequently paid, though excluded from the PPA salary base). Similarly, under subsection 127(26), any non-wage current SR&ED expenditure (e.g., contractor invoices, materials, or overhead) unpaid 180 days after year-end must be deducted from Qualified Expenditures on Line 528 of Form T661. Crucially, if an unpaid non-wage expenditure is not identified on Form T661 within the statutory 18-month reporting deadline for the year it was originally incurred, it can never be included in Qualified Expenditures to earn an ITC when paid in a future year.
5.4 Subcontractors, Non-Arm's-Length Contracts, and Third-Party Payments

The tax treatment of external R&D payments depends strictly on whether the payee is an arm's-length contractor, a non-arm's-length contractor, or an approved third-party entity. Where a claimant contracts an arm's-length taxable supplier (a person resident in Canada or a Canadian branch of a foreign corporation subject to Part I tax) to perform SR&ED in Canada on its behalf under subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i.01), 100% of the eligible current contract expenditure enters the subsection 37(1) deductible pool (Line 340), while 80% of the expenditure qualifies to earn an SR&ED ITC under subsection 127(9). To prevent duplication of ITCs, any "contract payment" received or receivable by the arm's-length contractor reduces the contractor's own Qualified Expenditures dollar-for-dollar under subsection 127(18) (though it does not reduce the contractor's subsection 37(1) deductible pool). If a contract involves SR&ED performed partially inside Canada and partially outside Canada, the claimant must reasonably allocate the contract price based on Fair Market Value; only the Canadian portion enters the subsection 37(1) pool and qualifies for the 80% ITC inclusion, whereas the foreign portion is ineligible for ITCs but deductible as a current expense under subsection 37(2). Furthermore, a payer may claim an arm's-length contract for paragraph 248(1)(d) support work only (such as specialized testing or machining) if the support work is commensurate with the needs and directly in support of core SR&ED performed by or on behalf of the payer in Canada, although the arm's-length support-work contractor cannot claim SR&ED on its own tax return because support work standing alone does not meet the definition of SR&ED.

Where a claimant enters into an SR&ED contract with a non-arm's-length (NAL) performer (such as a sister or subsidiary corporation), the contract payments are deductible by the payer in its subsection 37(1) pool (Line 345), but 0% qualifies for an ITC in the payer's hands. Instead, the NAL performer claims its own underlying SR&ED expenditures (where NAL contract receipts are excluded from the definition of "contract payment" and thus do not reduce the performer's QREs), and under subsection 37(13), support work performed by the NAL performer is linked to the payer's core SR&ED. Under subsection 127(13), the NAL performer and payer may jointly file prescribed Form T1146 (Agreement to Transfer Qualified Expenditures Incurred in Respect of SR&ED Contracts Between Persons Not Dealing at Arm's Length, updated May 15, 2026 to separate current transfers on Line 015 and post-December 15, 2024 capital transfers on Line 020) to transfer all or part of the performer's qualified expenditures to the payer, capped at the contract amount. Under the anti-avoidance rule in subsection 127(24), claimants cannot bypass the NAL rules by inserting an arm's-length intermediate party between the payer and a NAL subcontractor.

By contrast, Third-Party Payments under subparagraphs 37(1)(a)(i.1), (ii), and (iii) are payments made to approved universities, colleges, research institutes, approved associations, granting councils, or paragraph 149(1)(j) non-profit SR&ED corporations (or Canadian resident corporations under 37(1)(a)(i.1)) where the third party controls the SR&ED work and the payer is entitled to exploit the results on a non-exclusive preferential basis. Third-party payments are 100% deductible in the subsection 37(1) pool (Line 370) and 80% eligible for ITCs. Claimants must complete and attach Form T1263 (Third-Party Payments for SR&ED) for each payment. Unlike SR&ED contracts (which are accounted for on an accrual basis as the work is performed), third-party payments to Type B–F entities are recognized on a cash basis in the year paid, whereas payments to Type A entities (s. 37(1)(a)(i.1) Canadian resident corporations) are recognized on an accrual basis in the year the SR&ED is performed (paragraphs 18(9)(a) and (d)).
5.5 Materials Consumed vs. Materials Transformed

Under Regulation 2900(2)(a) (Traditional Method) and subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(V) (Proxy Method), the laid-down cost of physical, tangible materials (solid, liquid, or gaseous) used directly in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada is 100% deductible and 100% eligible for ITCs in the taxation year in which the material is consumed or transformed (not when purchased into inventory). Materials consumed (Line 320) are materials that are destroyed, absorbed, or rendered virtually valueless as a result of the SR&ED; if 90% or more of the value of a material is consumed in SR&ED, 100% of its cost qualifies as material consumed, whereas if experimental production is sold for more than 10% of its original cost, the materials are not considered consumed. General laboratory glassware and plastic ware (test tubes, pipettes, vials, beakers, flasks, dishes), cleaning supplies, CDs/DVDs, and general utilities (water, electricity, natural gas) are not considered "materials" for SR&ED. Materials transformed (Line 325) are materials incorporated into a prototype, pilot plant, custom product, or commercial asset that retains more than 10% of its value after the SR&ED. While 100% eligible when transformed, if the resulting property is subsequently sold or converted to commercial use within 20 years, the ITC Recapture rules (subsections 127(27) to 127(36)) claw back the ITC earned on the transformed materials. If materials are purchased from a non-arm's-length supplier, subsection 127(11.6) limits the qualified expenditure for ITC purposes to the NAL supplier's actual cost, excluding any intercompany profit mark-up.
5.6 Cloud Computing, Software Subscriptions, and Data Costs

In modern software, artificial intelligence (AI), machine learning, and data analytics SR&ED claims, improper classification of cloud computing infrastructure (e.g., AWS, Microsoft Azure, or Google Cloud Platform GPU training clusters) is one of the most frequent audit disallowances. Under the Proxy Method, actual overhead and indirect operating expenses are not identified or claimed on Form T661 because the notional 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount stands in for all overhead. Consequently, cloud computing invoices, SaaS development subscriptions, and server hosting costs cannot be claimed separately under the Proxy Method; if claimed alongside the 55% PPA, they are disallowed on assessment.

Conversely, under the Traditional Method, cloud computing and software subscription costs can be claimed as SR&ED overhead on Line 360 (Regulation 2900(2)(c)) if and only if they satisfy both the Directly Related test and the Incremental test. Standing commercial production cloud infrastructure (Cost of Goods Sold), general corporate SaaS licences, and fixed monthly internet, cellular, or telephone plans fail the incremental test because they would be incurred regardless of whether SR&ED was performed. However, a dedicated R&D cloud account or ephemeral GPU compute cluster provisioned specifically to execute experimental model training runs, billed separately or tracked with project tags, and shut down afterward satisfies both the directly related and incremental tests under the Traditional Method. Whenever a compute-heavy team's incremental R&D cloud spend plus other eligible Traditional overhead (such as employer related benefits for hands-on R&D personnel) exceeds 55% of its Proxy Salary Base, electing the Traditional Method produces a materially larger SR&ED claim than the Proxy Method.
5.7 Restored Capital Expenditures, Shared-Use Equipment (SUE), Equipment Lease Costs, and 20-Year ITC Recapture

For taxation years and property acquisitions after December 15, 2024, Bill C-15 restored three major capital and equipment incentives that had been repealed between January 1, 2014 and December 15, 2024:

items: SR&ED Capital Expenditures (ITA Paragraph 37(1)(b), Form T661 Line 390): Applies to new or used depreciable property (excluding land, buildings, or leasehold interests in buildings, except prescribed special-purpose buildings under Regulation 2903, and excluding General Purpose Office Equipment or Furniture under the Proxy Method) acquired and available for use (s. 37(1.2)) after December 15, 2024. The property must satisfy the All or Substantially All (ASA — ≥90%) test: at the time of acquisition, the claimant must intend that the property will be used during 90% or more of its operating time over its expected useful life in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada (subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(III) under Traditional; subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(III) under Proxy), OR that 90% or more of its value will be consumed in SR&ED in Canada. When eligible, 100% of the capital cost is added to the subsection 37(1) deductible pool on Line 390 and deemed to be separate CCA under subsection 37(6) (so it must not be included on Schedule T2SCH8). For new depreciable property, 100% of the cost is a Qualified Expenditure earning the 35% (40% refundable) or 15% ITC; used depreciable property is deductible on Line 390 in the subsection 37(1) pool, but is prescribed out of earning an ITC under Regulation 2902(b). Additionally, for general hardware and systems software that does not meet the 90% SR&ED test, Bill C-15 enacted immediate 100% first-year CCA expensing for Class 50 property acquired after April 15, 2024 and available for use before 2027.

Shared-Use Equipment (SUE — ITA Subsection 127(9), Form T661 Line 504 & Part 6C): New depreciable property acquired (available for use) after December 15, 2024 that does not meet the 90% ASA test—and is neither General Purpose Office Equipment or Furniture (GPOEF) nor Prescribed Depreciable Property (PDP) under Regulation 2900(11)—qualifies as SUE if it is used primarily (more than 50% of its actual operating time) for SR&ED in Canada. SUE is depreciated through regular CCA on Schedule T2SCH8 (not added to the subsection 37(1) pool), but earns an SR&ED ITC (under both Traditional and Proxy methods) on 25% (1/4) of its capital cost in the First Period (from the date available for use to the end of the first taxation year ending at least 12 months later) and an additional 25% (1/4) of its capital cost in the Second Period (from the date available for use to the end of the first taxation year ending at least 24 months later), for a combined qualified expenditure of 50% of capital cost. Claimants must report the 20 most expensive SUE properties in Part 6C of Form T661 (Boxes 788–796).

Equipment Lease Costs (Incurred After December 15, 2024 — Form T661 Line 350 / Line 360): Under the Traditional Method, lease costs incurred after December 15, 2024 for equipment used ASA (≥90% of operating time across the taxation year) in SR&ED are 100% claimable on Line 350 (subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(I)); if used less than 90% of the time, the actual SR&ED usage percentage is claimable as overhead on Line 360 if directly related and incremental (subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(II)). Under the Proxy Method (excluding GPOEF and land), lease costs incurred after December 15, 2024 are 100% claimable if used ASA (≥90% of operating time, subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(I)), 50% of the total lease cost if used primarily (>50% to <90% of operating time, subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(VI)), and 0% if used 50% or less of operating time. Outlays for the use of or right to use a building remain excluded under both methods unless the building is a prescribed special-purpose building under Regulation 2903.

20-Year Investment Tax Credit Recapture (ITA Subsections 127(27) to 127(36)): If a claimant disposes of, or converts to commercial use, any property on which an SR&ED ITC was earned—including ASA capital equipment, Shared-Use Equipment, animals/growing things, or transformed materials/prototypes—within 20 taxation years of acquisition (subsection 127(36) extending the 10-year rule in 127(27)(a) to 20 years), the claimant must add to its Part I tax payable for the year of disposition or conversion the lesser of the original ITC earned on the property and the historical ITC percentage multiplied by the proceeds of disposition (if sold at arm's length) or the Fair Market Value (if converted to commercial use or transferred at non-arm's length, with SUE recaptured on 25% or 50% of proceeds/FMV under subclauses 127(27)(f)(ii)(B) and (C)). No recapture applies to salaries, wages, or overhead; no recapture applies to the sale or licensing of Intellectual Property (IP); and under CRA administrative policy, no recapture is triggered on scrap sales or commercial conversions where proceeds or Fair Market Value are less than 10% of the original cost of the property. Any recaptured ITC added to Part I tax increases the claimant's subsection 37(1) deductible pool for the following taxation year under paragraph 37(1)(c.2).

body.text: 6.2 Detailed Provincial Regime Analysis
A. Québec: The New CRIC Regime vs. Eliminated Legacy Credits

In the March 25, 2025 Québec Budget, the Ministère des Finances enacted a comprehensive overhaul of provincial innovation tax incentives, replacing seven distinct tax measures with the single Tax Credit for R&D, Innovation and Pre-Commercialization (CRIC) (Crédit d'impôt pour la R-D et la précommercialisation, governed by sections 1029.8.21.16.1 to 1029.8.21.16.31 of the Taxation Act (Québec)) for taxation years or partnership fiscal periods beginning after March 25, 2025. The CRIC provides a 20% base refundable tax credit rate, which is increased up to 30% refundable on a maximum of $1,000,000 in eligible R&D and pre-commercialization expenditures that exceed the applicable exclusion threshold regardless of the corporation's asset size. For a taxation year or fiscal period, the applicable non-creditable exclusion threshold equals the greater of $50,000 or the sum of the corporation's R&D employees threshold and pre-commercialization employees threshold.

In addition to traditional R&D (which remains harmonized with the federal SR&ED definition and technically reviewed by the CRA), the CRIC covers pre-commercialization activities carried out in Québec as a continuation of Québec R&D—specifically: (1) testing, technological validation, and studies performed to satisfy regulatory requirements or obtain initial certification; (2) product design relating to form, aesthetics, functionality, or material selection; and (3) initial quality control activities for regulatory certification. Eligible CRIC costs include salaries and wages, subcontractor payments, payments to eligible research entities, and capital expenditures for the acquisition of depreciable property. Corporate claimants file Form RD-1029.8.CR-T (Tax Credit for R&D and Pre-Commercialization (CRIC)), alongside Form RD-1029.8.EN-T (Agreement Regarding the Expenditure Limit for the Tax Credit for R&D and Pre-Commercialization) and Form RD-1029.8.PR-T (Information Regarding the Pre-Commercialization Component).

For taxation years or fiscal periods beginning before March 26, 2025, claimants continue to file under the legacy rules using Form RD-222-V (Deduction Respecting SR&ED Expenditures) alongside the eliminated legacy credits: (1) the Tax Credit for Salaries and Wages (R&D) (Form RD-1029.7-V / CO-1029.8.36.DA); (2) the Tax Credit for University Research or Research Carried Out by a Public Research Centre or a Research Consortium (Form RD-1029.8.6-V); (3) the Tax Credit for Private Partnership Pre-Competitive Research (Form RD-1029.8.16.1-V, requiring a qualification certificate from the Minister of Economy, Innovation and Energy); and (4) the Tax Credit for Fees and Dues Paid to a Research Consortium (Form RD-1029.8.9.03-V, with a transitional rule allowing cumulative fee balances at the end of a period ending after March 25, 2025 to be claimed for taxation years ending no later than December 31, 2029). Québec also abolished the tax credit for technological adaptation services, the industrial design component of the design tax credits (retaining only fashion design), and the tax holiday for foreign researchers and experts. Furthermore, for taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025, Québec's patent box—the Deduction for the Commercialization of Innovations (DCI)—calculates its Québec nexus ratio using CRIC-eligible R&D expenditures (unreduced by the CRIC exclusion threshold, and excluding pre-commercialization costs). Separately, for fiscal years beginning in 2026, Québec replaced its legacy e-business salary credit (CDAE) with the CDAEIA (AI adoption credit), where the refundable portion starts at 22% in 2026 and steps down toward 20% by 2028 and requires AI integration.
B. Ontario: Tri-Credit Architecture (OITC, ORDTC, and OBRITC)

Ontario administers three distinct corporate R&D tax credits through the CRA under the Taxation Act, 2007 (Ontario). First, the Ontario Innovation Tax Credit (OITC — Section 96, Schedule T2SCH566) provides an 8% refundable tax credit (10% prior to June 1, 2016) to CCPCs with a permanent establishment in Ontario on up to $3,000,000 of qualified current SR&ED expenditures incurred in Ontario (maximum $240,000 annual cash refund). Associated corporations share the $3,000,000 limit, which phases out when prior-year federal taxable income is between $500,000 and $800,000 or prior-year specified paid-up capital is between $25,000,000 and $50,000,000. Unlike British Columbia, Ontario has not increased the OITC limit to $6,000,000, has not extended OITC to public corporations, and has not added restored federal capital expenditures to the OITC base.

Second, the Ontario Research and Development Tax Credit (ORDTC — Sections 38 to 45, Schedule T2SCH508) provides a 3.5% non-refundable tax credit (4.5% prior to June 1, 2016) on eligible Ontario SR&ED expenditures (after deducting OITC and OBRITC) to any corporation with an Ontario permanent establishment. Unused ORDTC carries back 3 years and forward 20 years. Because ORDTC is government assistance that reduces federal QREs and the subsection 37(1) pool in the year earned even if the corporation is in a tax-loss position and cannot use a non-refundable credit, a corporation may formally waive (renounce) all or part of its ORDTC by delivering a written waiver with its T2 return on or before 6 months after its taxation year-end (its filing-due date) or on an amended return for that year. Third, the Ontario Business-Research Institute Tax Credit (OBRITC — Section 97, Schedules T2SCH568 & T2SCH569) provides a 20% fully refundable tax credit on qualified expenditures incurred under an eligible contract with an eligible Ontario research institute (such as an Ontario university, college of applied arts and technology, or hospital research institute), subject to an annual expenditure cap of $20,000,000 (maximum $4,000,000 refund) shared across an associated corporate group.
C. British Columbia and Alberta

British Columbia enacted full legislative alignment with the federal Bill C-15 package for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024 under sections 97 to 103 of the Income Tax Act (British Columbia), claimed on Form T666 (Schedule 425 / S425). Qualifying CCPCs and Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) with a permanent establishment in B.C. earn a 10% refundable tax credit on up to $6,000,000 of qualifying B.C. current and restored capital SR&ED expenditures (up to $600,000 cash refund), phasing out over the $15,000,000 to $75,000,000 prior-year taxable capital (or 3-year revenue) range, while expenditures above the limit or incurred by other corporations earn a 10% non-refundable credit. Furthermore, B.C. Budget 2026 permanently repealed the statutory expiry date of the B.C. SR&ED credit.

In Alberta, the Innovation Employment Grant (IEG — Sections 26.95 to 26.99 of the Alberta Corporate Tax Act, AT1 Schedule 29 & Form AT4970) is administered directly by Alberta Treasury Board and Finance with a 15-month filing deadline after the AT1 filing-due date (21 months after taxation year-end). The IEG provides an 8% refundable payment on eligible Alberta R&D spending up to the corporation's base spending level (the average qualifying Alberta R&D spending over the preceding two taxation years) plus an additional 12% incremental payment (for a 20% combined refundable rate) on eligible spending exceeding that two-year base, up to an annual expenditure cap of $4,000,000. On June 30, 2026, Alberta published updated guidance confirming that the $4,000,000 cap and current-expenditure framework remain unchanged and providing directions for mapping expenditure amounts from the revised federal Form T661.
7. Government Assistance, Direct Grants (NRC IRAP, Strategic Response Fund), and Stacking Mechanics
7.1 Statutory Treatment of Government and Non-Government Assistance

Under paragraph 37(1)(d) and subsections 127(9), 127(18), 127(19), and 127(20) of the Income Tax Act, any government assistance (grants, subsidies, forgivable loans, investment allowances, or provincial/territorial R&D tax credits from a federal, provincial, municipal, Crown corporation, or foreign public authority, other than the federal SR&ED ITC itself) or non-government assistance (inducements or reimbursements included in income under paragraph 12(1)(x)) in respect of SR&ED reduces both the claimant's Pool of Deductible SR&ED Expenditures and its Qualified Expenditures for ITC purposes dollar-for-dollar. Consistent with accrual accounting, assistance must be deducted in the taxation year in which the claimant has received, is entitled to receive, or can reasonably be expected to receive the amount on or before the claimant's income tax return filing-due date for the year. Where assistance is received by a non-arm's-length party, it may be allocated to the performer using prescribed Form T1145 (Agreement to Allocate Assistance for SR&ED Between Persons Not Dealing at Arm's Length, updated May 15, 2026) under subsection 127(20).

When a claimant uses the Proxy Method, a portion of its provincial R&D tax credit (e.g., Ontario OITC/ORDTC or B.C. SR&ED) is earned on the notional 55% PPA. Because the PPA is never added to the subsection 37(1) deductible pool, the CRA's Assistance and Contract Payments Policy establishes that the portion of a provincial R&D tax credit attributable to the PPA does not reduce the subsection 37(1) pool (instead, it is included directly in business income under paragraph 12(1)(x) in the year received); however, under subsection 127(18), 100% of the provincial tax credit (including the PPA portion) does reduce federal Qualified Expenditures for calculating the federal SR&ED ITC. Conversely, when a company repays government or non-government assistance (such as repaying a conditional/repayable contribution from the Strategic Response Fund or a Regional Development Agency), paragraph 37(1)(c) adds the repayment to the subsection 37(1) deductible pool in the year of repayment, and subsections 127(10.7) and 127(10.8) generate an addition to the claimant's ITC calculated at the historical ITC rate that applied in the year the assistance originally reduced QREs. Because a repayment is not itself a "qualified expenditure" for the current year, the restored ITC is strictly non-refundable (it can only offset Part I tax or be carried back 3 years / forward 20 years).
7.2 Stacking SR&ED with NRC IRAP and the Strategic Response Fund (Formerly SIF)

The National Research Council of Canada Industrial Research Assistance Program (NRC IRAP) is Canada's premier direct R&D grant programme for incorporated, for-profit Canadian SMEs with 500 or fewer full-time equivalent employees. Delivered through Industrial Technology Advisors (ITAs), NRC IRAP provides non-repayable, cost-shared contributions toward R&D labour and Canadian subcontractors (with typical awards according to funding catalogues ranging up to $150,000–$1,000,000 and a $10,000,000 ceiling for major projects) alongside specialized streams such as IRAP AI Assist and Clean Technology renewals.

A critical statutory interaction makes stacking NRC IRAP and SR&ED under the Proxy Method highly advantageous. When calculating Form T661, the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) is computed in Part 5 on 100% of the gross eligible SR&ED salaries of directly engaged employees before government assistance (the NRC IRAP grant) is deducted in Part 4 (Line 532). For example, as illustrated in practitioner analyses, if a qualifying CCPC incurs $100,000 in directly engaged SR&ED salaries and receives an $80,000 (80%) non-repayable NRC IRAP grant toward those salaries, its gross eligible SR&ED salaries on Line 300 are $100,000 and its 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount on Line 820 / Line 502 is $55,000, yielding $155,000 in gross qualified expenditures before assistance. Subtracting the $80,000 NRC IRAP grant leaves $75,000 in net federal qualified SR&ED expenditures (comprising the $20,000 unsubsidized salary portion plus the full $55,000 notional PPA). At the 35% enhanced refundable ITC rate, the CCPC earns $26,250 in federal SR&ED cash refunds on top of the $80,000 NRC IRAP grant, recovering $106,250 (106.25% of the $100,000 cash payroll outlay) before adding provincial R&D tax credits.

At the large-enterprise scale, the Strategic Response Fund (SRF)—which replaced the Strategic Innovation Fund (SIF) (originally launched in 2017) with a $5 billion investment announced in 2025, and which received a new $1 billion commitment over six years starting in 2028–29 in Federal Budget 2026—provides repayable and non-repayable anchor contributions (minimum $10 million contribution on projects of $20 million or more) across AI, agri-food, bio-manufacturing, and clean technologies. All SRF/SIF contributions attributable to SR&ED expenditures must be deducted as government assistance under paragraph 37(1)(d) and subsection 127(18) in the year received or receivable, and any subsequent repayments generate non-refundable ITC restorations under subsections 127(10.7) and 127(10.8).
8. Filing Procedures, Prescribed Forms, Statutory Deadlines, and CRA Audit Defence
8.1 Prescribed Forms and Line-by-Line Structure of Form T661

To access SR&ED deductions and ITCs, a claimant must file Form T661 (Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Expenditures Claim, updated May 15, 2026) together with Schedule T2SCH31 (for corporations, updated May 22, 2026) or Form T2038(IND) (for individuals and trusts) along with their income tax return.
