body.text: For each claimed project, the technical narrative in Form T661 Part 2, Section B must be prepared by technical personnel familiar with the work within strict statutory word ceilings: Line 242 (What scientific or technological uncertainties did you attempt to overcome?) has a maximum of 350 words; Line 244 (What work did you perform in the tax year to overcome the scientific or technological uncertainties described in Line 242?) has a maximum of 700 words; and Line 246 (What scientific or technological advancements did you achieve or attempt to achieve as a result of the work described in Line 244?) has a maximum of 350 words. If a federal agency has designated a project as "classified information" for national security reasons, the claimant completes Section B of Part 2 on a separate sheet retained in its records and submits a notification letter to the CRA rather than transmitting the classified technical text with the return.

Under subsection 37(11)(b) and subsections 162(5.1), 162(5.2), and 162(5.3) of the Income Tax Act, every claimant must also complete Part 9 of Form T661 disclosing whether a "claim preparer" (any person or partnership that accepts consideration to prepare or assist in preparing the claim) participated in the filing, along with the preparer's Business Number, billing arrangement code (such as a contingency fee percentage, flat fee, or hourly rate; published practitioner fee guides note that market contingency fees typically range from 15% to 25% of the credit), and total fee paid or payable. If no external claim preparer was used, the claimant must still complete Lines 935, 970, and 975 in Part 9. If required claim preparer information is omitted, incomplete, or false, subsection 162(5.1) imposes a $1,000 penalty for which the claimant and the claim preparer are jointly and severally, or solidarily, liable, subject to a due-diligence defence under subsection 162(5.2). Note that the claim preparer disclosure in Part 9 (and the decision to deduct amounts from an already-established subsection 37(1) pool) is not subject to the 18-month disallowance rule that governs project expenditures.
8.2 The Absolute 18-Month Statutory Reporting Deadline

Under subsections 37(11), 37(11.1), and 37(12) (for the deductible pool) and paragraph (m) of the definition of "investment tax credit" in subsection 127(9) (for the ITC), prescribed forms containing the prescribed project and expenditure information must be filed on or before the day that is 12 months after the taxpayer's income tax return filing-due date for the taxation year in which the expenditure was incurred. Because a corporate T2 return is due 6 months after the end of the taxation year (paragraph 150(1)(a)), a corporation's absolute SR&ED reporting deadline is 18 months after the end of its taxation year (for example, a December 31, 2024 taxation year-end has a T2 filing-due date of June 30, 2025, and an absolute SR&ED reporting deadline of June 30, 2026). For individuals carrying on a sole proprietorship (whose T1 filing-due date is June 15), the SR&ED reporting deadline is 17.5 months after the December 31 calendar year-end (June 15 of the second following year), and for trusts (whose T3 return is due 90 days after year-end), the deadline is 90 days plus 12 months after the trust's taxation year-end.

If the prescribed forms or prescribed line-item information are not filed on or before the 18-month reporting deadline, the CRA cannot by law grant any extension of time. The ministerial "taxpayer relief" provisions in subsection 220(3.1) of the Income Tax Act only permit waivers of penalties and interest and cannot be used to accept or revive a late-filed Form T661 or Schedule T2SCH31. Under subsection 37(11.1) and subsection 37(12), any expenditure not reported on Form T661 with its prescribed information by the 18-month deadline is permanently deemed not to be an expenditure on or in respect of SR&ED. If a claimant files Form T661 on time with complete prescribed information for some projects but omits prescribed information for another project past the 18-month deadline, the CRA accepts the compliant projects and disallows only the project with missing prescribed information. Furthermore, if Form T661 is filed on time, but Schedule T2SCH31 / Form T2038(IND) is not filed by the 18-month deadline, the claimant may add the allowable expenditures to its subsection 37(1) Pool of Deductible SR&ED Expenditures, but cannot earn any ITCs. Conversely, if Schedule T2SCH31 / Form T2038(IND) is filed on time, but Form T661 is not filed by the 18-month deadline, the claimant cannot deduct any SR&ED expenditures, cannot add them to the subsection 37(1) pool, and cannot earn any ITCs.
8.3 Pre-Claim Approval, CRA Audit Review Procedures, and Dispute Resolution

Building on its earlier Pre-Claim Consultation (PCC) and Pre-Claim Review (PCR) services, the CRA launched a formal optional Pre-Claim Approval process on April 1, 2026. Through an online application submitted via My Business Account prior to starting work or filing a claim, a business can obtain an upfront determination from the CRA on whether its planned R&D projects qualify as SR&ED within eight weeks (with one-on-one information sessions available via OESCPB-SVEDGPO@cra-arc.gc.ca). Under The SR&ED Review Process: A Guide for Claimants (updated April 20, 2026), if a claim containing pre-approved projects is subsequently selected for post-filing review, the CRA processes it under one of three scenarios: (1) an Expenditure-Only Review processed generally within 90 calendar days of receiving the complete claim; (2) a Work and Expenditure Review under the standard 180-calendar-day timeline if the executed projects differed significantly from what was approved during pre-claim approval; or (3) a standard 180-calendar-day review if the claim also includes projects that did not receive pre-claim approval.

For regular refundable SR&ED claims selected for review, the CRA's official service standard is 180 calendar days from the date the CRA receives a complete claim (which the CRA commits to meeting 90% of the time; unreviewed refundable claims are generally processed in about 60 days), whereas there is no service standard for processing non-refundable SR&ED claims selected for review. Once an SR&ED claim is selected for review, it cannot be withdrawn, as Form T661 forms part of the tax return and the Part 10 certification cannot be revoked. Reviews are conducted jointly (primarily via virtual videoconferencing and screen sharing, with on-site premises tours conducted where necessary to inspect ASA equipment, SUE usage logs, prototypes, and the scrap yard) by a Research and Technology Advisor (RTA)—who evaluates technical eligibility under subsection 248(1), reports to a Research and Technology Manager (RTM), and prepares the SR&ED Project Eligibility Report—and a Financial Reviewer (FR), who verifies accounting records, payroll, contracts, and assistance, reports to a Financial Review Manager (FRM), and prepares the 10-section Financial Review Report (FRR). Under the CRA Claim Review Manual, RTAs are strictly prohibited from negotiating eligibility or trading project acceptances for percentage reductions, though RTAs and FRs may establish a documented reasonable estimate where SR&ED was proven to have occurred but boundary records are imprecise. Under the Financial Claim Review Manual, every audit adjustment in Section E of the FRR must cite specific statutory subsections and establish both a primary and secondary legal basis for reassessment. Under subsection 230(1) and paragraph 230(4)(b) of the Income Tax Act, claimants must retain all financial books and contemporaneous technical records supporting an SR&ED claim for 6 years from the end of the last taxation year to which the records relate.

When the RTA and FR propose negative adjustments to a claim (or propose penalties), the CRA issues a Proposal Package comprising the SR&ED Project Eligibility Report, a Proposal Letter, and financial adjustment schedules. The claimant has 30 calendar days from the date of the Proposal Letter to submit written representations and supporting documentation. If concerns persist during the review, the claimant follows the CRA's three-step administrative dispute resolution process:

items: Step 1 — Discuss with the Reviewers: Address technical and financial findings directly with the assigned RTA and/or FR.
Step 2 — Escalate to Review Managers: Escalate unresolved technical or financial disagreements to the Research and Technology Manager (RTM) and/or Financial Review Manager (FRM).

Step 3 — Request an Administrative Review: After receiving the Proposal Package, request a formal Administrative Review to verify whether the review complied with SR&ED legislation, policies, procedures, and due process (note that an Administrative Review is not a second technical review by new reviewers).

body.text: If the CRA maintains its disallowance and issues a formal Notice of Assessment or Notice of Reassessment, the claimant has the statutory right to file a formal Notice of Objection within 90 days from the date of the Notice of Assessment or Reassessment, followed by a statutory appeal to the Tax Court of Canada.
9. Landmark Canadian SR&ED Jurisprudence and Audit Precedents

Canadian tax courts have developed a rigorous body of jurisprudence interpreting subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act. Because CRA administrative guidelines are not legally binding on the judiciary, tax auditors and legal counsel must evaluate every SR&ED claim against the binding precedents of the Tax Court of Canada (TCC) and the Federal Court of Appeal (FCA).

body.text: 9.1 Detailed Case Law Analysis for Audit Defence

In Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Limited v. The Queen (98 DTC 1839), Judge Bowman established the five-question analytical framework that governs every SR&ED dispute in Canada: (1) Is there a technical risk or uncertainty that cannot be removed by routine engineering or standard procedures? (2) Did the person claiming to be doing SR&ED formulate hypotheses specifically aimed at reducing or eliminating that technological uncertainty (requiring observation of the problem, formulation of a clear objective, identification of the uncertainty, formulation of hypotheses, and methodical testing)? (3) Did the procedures adopted accord with established and objective principles of the scientific method, characterized by trained and systematic observation, measurement and experiment, and the formulation, testing, and modification of hypotheses? (4) Did the process result in a technological advancement? and (5) Was a detailed record of the hypotheses, tests, and results kept contemporaneously as the work progressed?.

In National R&D Inc. v. Canada (2022 FCA 72)—where an SR&ED consulting firm claimed credits for its 2011 taxation year in respect of a web-based, cross-platform, and cross-browser software project titled "Project Tracking System"—the appellant argued that the third criterion of Northwest Hydraulic ("total discipline of the scientific method") had no textual foundation in subsection 248(1) and was inconsistent with the CRA's August 2021 "Why and How" Guidelines. Writing for the Federal Court of Appeal, Justice Donald Rennie rejected the argument (citing Kam-Press Metal Products Ltd. v. Canada, 2021 FCA 88), holding that Parliament relies on the courts to provide definition and precision to statutory text, that CRA administrative commentary is not binding on the courts, and that even though the 2021 CRA Guidelines omitted the exact phrase "scientific method," the "How" requirement still enforces "an underlying rigour or discipline in the experimental process". Because National R&D's documentation was found to be vague, unclear, and lacking a logical progression from premise to experimental results, the denial of the claim was upheld, and the Supreme Court of Canada subsequently rejected the taxpayer's application for leave to appeal.

Taxpayers also frequently conflate commercial cost targets with technological uncertainty. In 6398316 Canada Inc. v. The Queen (2021 TCC 17), the appellant constructed a grid-independent home in 2012–2013 designed to maintain a constant indoor temperature using natural environmental fluctuations at the same construction cost as a conventional home. The Tax Court of Canada dismissed the appeal, holding that achieving a cost target is an economic concern rather than a technological uncertainty. However, as Justice Lafleur observed (referencing earlier jurisprudence) and the CRA's 2021 Guidelines on the Eligibility of Work confirm, business and economic constraints are relevant background factors when they impose interlocking constraints that force engineers to abandon conventional materials or designs and resolve genuine technological obstacles. In preparing Form T661 Line 242, claimants must frame their hypotheses and uncertainties strictly around the physical, chemical, biological, or computational obstacles rather than price or budget targets.

Finally, across Sass Manufacturing (88 DTC 1363), RIS-Christie (99 DTC 5087), and C.W. Agencies (2001 FCA 393), the courts have consistently ruled that oral testimony or retrospective expert reconstruction prepared during an audit or litigation cannot cure a lack of contemporaneous documentation generated while the R&D was underway. At the same time, the Tax Court of Canada's 2024 decision in Manning Canning Kitchens Inc. (2024 TCC 159) (where a food processor conducted systematic experimentation to control microbial growth in a room-temperature shelf-stable vinegar-based drink) provides an important precedent for SMEs: Justice Bodie held that technological uncertainty can be established even where publicly known preservatives exist if they have never been used in the specific context, and clarified that contemporaneous documentation is meant to track the hypotheses generated, experiments undertaken, and results obtained by the team as work progressed rather than be written for an external person unfamiliar with the field to replicate the results.
10. Comprehensive Verification Checklist for Canadian SR&ED Claimants (2026 Filing Cycle)

To ensure full statutory compliance and audit readiness under the enacted 2026 rules, Canadian corporate and unincorporated claimants should verify the following ten audit checkpoints prior to submitting their return:

items: Taxation Year Start-Date Verification: Confirm whether the taxation year began after December 15, 2024 to apply the $6,000,000 expenditure limit, the $15,000,000 to $75,000,000 phase-out range, and ECPC eligibility on Part 10B of Schedule T2SCH31.

CCPC Revenue Election Optimization (Subsections 127(10.31) and 127(10.32)): If the claimant is a CCPC (or member of an associated CCPC group) whose prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada exceeds $15,000,000, calculate its three-year average annual gross revenue; if average revenue is lower than taxable capital, elect on Schedule T2SCH31 (Line 383) and Schedule T2SCH52 to compute the $6,000,000 expenditure limit under the revenue formula in subsection 127(10.6).

Proxy vs. Traditional Method Arithmetic Audit: Verify that the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) is computed at 55% of the Salary Base (Regulation 2900(4)). If the company incurred substantial incremental R&D cloud computing costs (AWS/Azure/GCP GPU training clusters) and employer related benefits that exceed 55% of the Proxy Salary Base, elect the Traditional Method (Line 162) on initial filing, as cloud costs are strictly disallowed under the Proxy Method and the method election is irrevocable.

Specified Employee Cap Compliance: Identify all ≥10% shareholders and non-arm's-length employees; strip 100% of their bonuses and profit-based remuneration from Line 305 (s. 37(9)), cap their deductible SR&ED wages at 5 × YMPE prorated by days (s. 37(9.1)), cap their Part 5 Proxy Salary Base inclusion at the lesser of 75% of total salary or 2.5 × YMPE prorated by days (Reg 2900(7)), and file Form T1174 if employed across associated corporations.

Post-December 15, 2024 Capital, Lease, and SUE Segregation: Segregate all depreciable property acquired (available for use) and equipment lease costs incurred after December 15, 2024. Claim new ASA (≥90%) equipment on Line 390 (removing it from Schedule T2SCH8 CCA), claim new Shared-Use Equipment (>50% SR&ED operating time) at 25% per term on Line 504 / Part 6C, and claim eligible equipment lease costs on Line 350 (100% if ASA ≥90%; 50% under Proxy if >50% to <90%).

180-Day Unpaid Amounts Scrubbing: Reconcile accrued year-end payroll bonuses and accounts payable ledgers to identify any SR&ED wages (s. 78(4)) or current contractor/material expenses (s. 127(26)) unpaid 180 days after taxation year-end, reporting unpaid non-wage current costs on Line 528 before the 18-month deadline so they remain eligible for ITCs when paid in a future year.

Provincial Regime Alignment and ORDTC Waiver Analysis: File Form T666 (Schedule 425) in British Columbia to capture the $6,000,000 limit and restored capital expenditures; file Forms RD-1029.8.CR-T and RD-222-V with Revenu Québec for taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025 to claim the 20%–30% CRIC on R&D, pre-commercialization, and capital costs; and in Ontario, evaluate whether to waive the 3.5% non-refundable ORDTC (Schedule T2SCH508) by the 6-month T2 filing-due date if the corporation cannot utilize non-refundable Ontario tax credits, preventing an unnecessary government assistance reduction to the 35% refundable federal SR&ED ITC.

NRC IRAP and Government Assistance Sequencing: Deduct all non-repayable grants (NRC IRAP) and provincial R&D tax credits received, receivable, or reasonably expected by the filing-due date on Part 4 (Lines 529–535), while ensuring that under the Proxy Method, the 55% PPA in Part 5 is computed on 100% of gross eligible SR&ED salaries prior to subtracting the NRC IRAP grant.

Part 9 Claim Preparer Verification: Complete all required lines in Part 9 of Form T661 (or Lines 935, 970, and 975 if prepared entirely in-house) to avoid the $1,000 joint-and-several penalty under subsection 162(5.1).

Strict 18-Month Calendar Tracking: Submit the complete Form T661 and Schedule T2SCH31 / Form T2038(IND) well in advance of the 18-month corporate reporting deadline (subsection 37(11) and paragraph 127(9)(m)), recognizing that the deadline is statutory and cannot be extended or waived under any administrative provision.
